ai.subject: Anatomy
ai.summary: The Circle of Willis is a ring of arteries at the brain’s base that provides collateral flow, protecting against ischemia. Its branch points are prone to berry aneurysms, which can rupture into the subarachnoid space.

sections.p: A circular arterial anastomosis at the brain base, formed by the internal carotid, anterior cerebral, posterior cerebral, and communicating arteries. It ensures continuous blood supply if one pathway is blocked.

Situated at the skull base, the circle is composed of the anterior communicating artery (ACoA), two anterior cerebral arteries (ACAs), two internal carotid arteries (ICAs), two posterior communicating arteries (PCoAs), and two posterior cerebral arteries (PCAs).
b: ICAs give rise to ACAs and PCoAs

sections.p: Surrounded by the optic chiasm, pituitary stalk, and cavernous sinuses. The circle lies just above the brainstem and below the tentorium cerebelli.
Arises from the internal carotid and basilar arteries. The circle’s anastomoses allow redistribution of blood if a major artery is occluded.
No direct nerve supply; however, its proximity to cranial nerves (III, IV, VI) and the optic chiasm means ischemia can affect vision and eye movements.
Maintains cerebral perfusion by providing alternative routes for blood flow, reducing the risk of ischemic stroke when a major artery is compromised.
Berry aneurysms form at arterial branch points, especially the ACoA and PCoAs. Rupture leads to subarachnoid hemorrhage, a life‑threatening emergency.

t.b: Detects acute subarachnoid hemorrhage; a positive finding indicates aneurysm rupture.
Visualises aneurysm size and location; guides surgical or endovascular treatment.
Elevated opening pressure and xanthochromia confirm subarachnoid bleeding when CT is negative.

sections.p: Remember the circle’s key arteries and that the ACoA is the most common aneurysm site. In a patient with sudden severe headache, think subarachnoid hemorrhage and order CT first.
Treat the underlying cause (e.g., hypertension control). Surgical clipping or endovascular coiling stops bleeding. Supportive care includes intracranial pressure control and seizure prophylaxis.
The basilar artery and vertebral arteries are separate; the circle is not a single vessel but an anastomotic ring.
b: Basilar artery is not part of the circle

sections.p: Early CT may miss small aneurysms; lumbar puncture can be falsely normal if performed too early.
Urgent care is needed for sudden severe headache, neck stiffness, or altered consciousness.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden severe headache with neck stiffness

faq.a: A small, berry‑shaped dilation at an arterial branch point, most often in the Circle of Willis; it can rupture into the subarachnoid space.

faq.q: Why does the Circle of Willis matter clinically?
faq.a: It provides collateral flow, protecting the brain from ischemia if a major artery is blocked.

faq.q: How is a ruptured aneurysm diagnosed?
faq.a: CT head without contrast is first; if negative but suspicion remains, lumbar puncture or CT angiography is performed.
